posts.raw_content:
Hey everyone,

Looking for some honest perspective from fellow believers on a situation my girlfriend and I are navigating.

We have been attending a local Baptist church since Easter. Because of our work schedules, Sunday mornings are pretty much all we can consistently attend for regular services, but we have made an effort to get involved in fellowship activities outside of that. Early on, it seemed promising. The pastor and I exchanged numbers, we had one-on-one conversations, he has been over to our house, and we have been over to his.

On paper, having that kind of direct access to a pastor sounds great. But over the last several months, between the preaching, personal interactions, church events, and now a sudden push for membership, I have gone from feeling uneasy to being thoroughly alarmed. What started as basic, shallow preaching has devolved into a passive-aggressive personality cult that uses spiritual manipulation to demand total compliance.

Here is the full picture of what has unfolded:

1. Therapeutic preaching and safe storytelling
When we first started attending, he was preaching on godly men and women from Proverbs and similar passages. It was basic, but it felt good enough, and he is an engaging storyteller. At first, it was entertaining, and I felt like I was picking things up. Over time, the pattern became undeniable: zero preaching on sin, repentance, judgment, or hell. Nothing addresses the dark times we live in, and nothing touches anything remotely controversial. Even visiting missionaries give safe, milk-toast messages. The overarching message from the pulpit is spiritual therapy: Jesus just wants to help you through your week, fix your problems, and make you feel better. His sermons are about 10% Bible and 90% stories and jokes. In his most recent sermon, he referenced stories from Scripture without even bothering to open the text and read the Word of God with the congregation. How could anyone sitting in those pews know their Bible deeply when they are being fed human anecdotes instead of the Word of God?

2. A bizarre, controlled dynamic at the men's meeting
I recently attended a men’s meeting, excited to see what godly brotherhood looked like. We gathered, joked around, prayed, the pastor read a brief passage, told a story, opened the floor for questions/verses, and then did some physical labor around the church (the free labor was whatever, I didn't mind helping out).

What bothered me was the dynamic in the room. When it came to corporate prayer, everyone kept it entirely safe and generic, unless it was for a sick relative. A few guys prayed for the Lord to "send laborers into the harvest field," yet here was a room full of able-bodied men refusing to do any actual corporate evangelism in their own community, expecting someone far away to do the heavy lifting. It felt hollow. Worse, the social pressure was palpable: any serious question digging into Scripture or touching controversial ground would clearly be shut down. Anyone questioning the pastor would instantly be labeled a rebel. It was bizarre watching grown men laugh on cue at every single joke the pastor made, even when none of them were funny. He is subtly idolized, exercising total control over the atmosphere. It did not feel like authentic Christian fellowship; it felt like a personality cult where men stay surface-level because going deeper is actively discouraged.

3. Total apathy toward corporate evangelism
When I asked him directly about community outreach, he told me flat out that he does not believe the church as a corporate body should do evangelism. His stance is that it is strictly an individual duty. His reasoning? He used to go door-to-door, but stopped because "people just think you're Mormons." To hear a Baptist pastor abandon church-led outreach out of social awkwardness and fear of being mistaken for a cult was shocking.

4. Shrugging off blatant heresy
I brought up the controversy surrounding James Talarico’s pastor, who publicly claimed that the Virgin Birth was just a myth and that "it doesn't matter what you believe" as long as you love people. Denying the Virgin Birth strikes right at the heart of the Incarnation, the sinless nature of Christ, and the authority of Scripture. I expected a pastor to show some righteous concern or defend basic orthodoxy. Instead, he brushed it off, saying people just tell others what they want to hear, and that "it will matter what they believe when they die." It was total apathy, with zero pastoral vigilance against wolves or false doctrine.

5. Dodging apologetics and historical substance
I brought up historical questions regarding religious origins (specifically historical arguments around Muhammad versus the solid historical evidence for Jesus Christ). Rather than engaging, he brushed it aside, claiming people say the same thing about Jesus, and shut the conversation down immediately. He clearly had no appetite to discuss apologetics, history, or the defense of the faith.

6. Sidestepping basic doctrine
Wanting to see where we stood and ensure we were on the same page doctrinally, I texted him an outline of my core theological beliefs. He never responded to the text. Instead, he showed up at my front door a day later to hand me a lukewarm, generic devotional book without ever addressing what I wrote. It was a completely intentional dodge to avoid a serious doctrinal conversation while keeping things superficially pleasant.

7. The tipping point: High-control membership and spiritual manipulation
I had been trying to extend grace and overlook these faults, but during his current series on basic doctrine, he got to the section on church membership, and the mask came completely off.

According to him, being a born-again believer and a member of the universal body of Christ is not enough. Coming faithfully on Sunday mornings and attending fellowship events is not enough. You must sign a church contract, tithe your money, and be present at every single service—Sunday morning, Sunday night, and Wednesday night—or else you are outside of God's blessing.

He explicitly preaches that you need the pastor for spiritual protection. He openly scoffs at people who miss services and struggle with problems, claiming that if they had just shown up to his service, they would have been blessed. Blessed by what? His 90% stories and unfunny jokes? He lectures about how essential fellowship with the brethren is, but what does that fellowship actually consist of? Saying hi, asking about work, and talking about the weather for five minutes in the lobby. How is that edifying anyone? Most of the congregation are passive pew warmers with near-zero biblical knowledge and no discernment. If they had any grounding in Scripture, they would be as alarmed as I am.

He claims you have to sign this contract to be a voting member. Why does that matter? I would vote that he actually open the Bible and preach the Word, but that would never be permitted on the docket.

It feels like you are not allowed to simply be saved, pray, read your Bible, attend worship, and give. You have to sign on the dotted line, surrender your critical thinking, treat the pastor like an untouchable guru, hand over your wallet, and become a compliant cog who never makes demands and never asks hard questions.

How on earth is this functionally different from a cult?

I do not expect a pastor to be perfect, but a shepherd is called to preach the whole counsel of God, guard the flock from error, and equip the saints for battle—not build a localized fiefdom where an unchallenged leader keeps everyone spiritually stunted on feel-good stories while demanding blind obedience.

Has anyone else walked through this specific bait-and-switch where a church seems normal at first, only to reveal high-control legalism underneath? Is there any point in even confronting this, or is this a situation where we need to dust our boots off and leave immediately?

I would appreciate any grounded perspective from fellow believers.
